causes.text: Crude oil prices plunged about 25% after Saudi Arabia and Russia launched a price war when their production pact collapsed, flooding the market with supply and causing the biggest one-day drop since the Gulf War.

source_info.title: Oil plunges 25%, hit by erupting Saudi-Russia oil price war

effects.text: Chevron cut its 2020 capital spending by $4 billion to $16 billion, suspended its $5 billion annual share buyback program after repurchasing $1.75 billion in Q1, and reduced planned Permian output by roughly 125,000 boe/d in response to the price crash.

source_info.title: Chevron leads another wave of massive oil-industry spending cuts

causal_reasoning_chain.description: Saudi Arabia and Russia abandoned their supply pact and launched an oil price war, triggering a massive oversupply and causing crude prices to fall by roughly 25% in a day.
The sudden slump in benchmark prices slashed producers' expected cash flows, forcing oil majors to reevaluate budgets and capital expenditure.
Chevron responded by cutting 2020 capex by $4 billion to $16 billion, suspending buybacks and lowering Permian output plans.
On March 24, 2020, investors viewed the cuts as prudent; Chevron's shares jumped about 21% to $65.73 that day.

rationale: The Saudi-Russia price war precipitated an abrupt collapse in oil prices, compressing expected cash flows for producers. Chevron's capex and output reductions directly reflect this shock and were interpreted by markets as balance-sheet protective actions.
counterfactual_analysis: Had Saudi Arabia and Russia maintained their production agreement, the supply shock and price collapse likely would have been avoided or moderated; Chevron may not have needed to slash capex or adjust output plans.

adversarial_confounders.text: The COVID-19 pandemic simultaneously curbed global oil demand
adversarial_confounders.impact: Demand destruction from lockdowns also pressured prices and could independently explain Chevron's spending cuts.

details.commentary: Aggressive production competition among dominant oil exporters kept supply high, eroding OPEC's ability to defend prices. For integrated majors like Chevron, this dynamic limited pricing power and margin expansion, leading investors to temper their expectations for future profitability.
